items.title: Perceived Ratings of AI-Generated and Expert-Reviewed vs Clinician-Developed Virtual Cardiology Patient Scenarios Among Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Virtual patients (VPs) are widely used in medical education, but creating high-quality cases requires clinical expertise, iterative revision, and alignment with educational objectives. Generative AI may support VP authoring, but direct comparisons between AI-generated and clinician-developed cases delivered within the same educational setting remain limited. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to compare medical students’ learner-perceived ratings of 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed virtual cardiology patient scenario with those of 1 clinician-developed virtual cardiology patient scenario delivered through the same mobile platform. METHODS A randomized, participant-blinded 2-arm controlled study was conducted in October 2025 during scheduled fifth-year emergency medicine course sessions. Eligible participants were fifth-year medical students who had completed the cardiology course. Students were assigned 1:1 to complete either a clinician-developed VP (CD-VP; n=64) or a ChatGPT-generated VP (GPT-VP; n=67). Both scenarios followed a shared acute coronary syndrome blueprint and were delivered through the same mobile-optimized app (mobile VPs app [MobiViP]) with identical interface structure and branching logic. The GPT-VP was generated using GPT-5 and refined through iterative follow-up prompting under expert review; direct manual rewriting was prohibited. After completion, students completed a mandatory 19-item questionnaire covering realism and validity, cognitive load, self-reported learning and reflection, and engagement and satisfaction. Analyses included reliability testing, 1-sample tests against a neutral midpoint, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Spearman correlations. Full scenario content and development details are provided as multimedia appendices. RESULTS A total of 131 complete questionnaires were analyzed, with no item-level missing data. Mean subscale scores in the CD-VP group were 3.81 (SD 0.64) for realism and validity, 3.67 (SD 0.74) for cognitive load, 3.64 (SD 0.73) for self-reported learning and reflection, and 4.16 (SD 0.64) for engagement and satisfaction; corresponding GPT-VP scores were 4.11 (SD 0.56), 3.03 (SD 0.76), 3.86 (SD 0.77), and 4.28 (SD 0.58), respectively. Compared with the CD-VP, the GPT-VP received higher ratings for realism and validity (Mann-Whitney U=1503.0; P=.003) and lower cognitive load ratings, indicating a lower perceived burden (Mann-Whitney U=1070.5; P<.001). Self-reported learning and reflection showed a marginal difference between groups, with a higher rating for the GPT-VP (Mann-Whitney U=1719.0; P=.05), whereas engagement and satisfaction did not differ significantly (Mann-Whitney U=1922.5; P=.31). Internal consistency was acceptable to good for most subscales, although internal consistency for the realism and validity subscale in the GPT-VP group was moderate (Cronbach α=0.67). CONCLUSIONS In this single-center randomized study, 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed cardiology VP scenario was rated similarly to or more favorably than 1 clinician-developed scenario in selected learner-perceived domains. Future research should expand to objective learning, retention, development workload, and scalability outcomes.

items.title: Performance Management and Workforce Analytics in Tourism
items.abstract: The fast adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism management has fundamentally changed the way organizations handle human resources, performance, and utilize workforce data. This chapter explains how AI-based performance management systems and workforce analytics can be used in a versatile way in the tourism and hospitality industries. It relies on current empirical data and theoretical ideas to explore how machine learning algorithms, predictive analytics, and real-time data platforms are changing talent acquisition, employee performance appraisal, demand-based scheduling, and strategic workforce planning. The chapter also discusses the ethical issues of algorithmic bias, privacy, and employee autonomy, and the need to adopt hybrid human-AI governance frameworks. The practical implementation results are reflected in the case studies of large global tourism enterprises. The chapter ends with a discussion of future research directions and policy implications of sustainable, technology-enhanced people management in tourism.

items.title: Perioperative hemostatic therapy in adult cardiac surgery: a narrative review highlighting human factors: A narrative review highlighting human factors
items.abstract: Severe bleeding remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in cardiac surgery, and hemostatic blood components, mainly platelet concentrates and fresh frozen plasma, are essential to perioperative hemostatic management. While restrictive strategies for packed red blood cell transfusions are now well established within Patient Blood Management, inappropriate prophylactic transfusions of these hemostatic therapies continue to receive less attention. This narrative review investigates variations in hemostatic therapy among centres for adult cardiac surgery, and examines the factors that might explain these differences. A review of fourteen original studies involving nearly 220,000 patients from over 1,000 centres worldwide revealed significant variations in platelet and fresh-frozen plasma transfusion rates across centres. Differences in patient and procedural characteristics cannot entirely explain these variations. Although viscoelastic hemostatic tests have improved bedside assessment and lowered exposure in some settings, they have not eradicated significant variations in practice. The available evidence indicates that hospital culture, local organization, transfusion thresholds, and human factors all have an impact on transfusion behaviour. Optimizing the use of hemostatic therapies in adult cardiac surgery will therefore not only require better tools and protocols, but also increased focus on the organizational and non-technical factors that influence decision-making.

items.title: Perspective Chapter: Digital versus Traditional Autopsy in Forensic Practice – Techniques, Applications and Future Directions
items.abstract: Autopsy, as a cornerstone of post-mortem investigation, has undergone significant evolution over the years. Traditional autopsy, characterised by manual examination and tissue sampling, has long been the gold standard for determining the cause of death and uncovering underlying pathologies. However, the emergence of digital autopsy, leveraging advanced imaging techniques and computational analysis, presents a promising alternative. This chapter provides a comprehensive comparison between traditional and digital autopsy, encompassing their methodologies, diagnostic accuracy, practicality, limitations, and ethical considerations. It focuses on how digital tools such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and digital imaging and communications in medicine (DICOM)-based visualisation reconstruct the human body’s structure into detailed, colour-coded three-dimensional models of the internal organs. The chapter further examines the impact of technological advancement on forensic pathology and explores the integration of digitalisation, artificial intelligence, and minimally invasive techniques into routine post-mortem practice. Its novelty lies in bringing conventional dissection-based autopsy and digital/virtual autopsy together within a single comparative framework, and in extending that framework to artificial intelligence and minimally invasive sampling. By elucidating the strengths and limitations of both approaches, it aims to guide forensic practitioners, pathologists, radiologists, policymakers, and researchers in making informed decisions regarding post-mortem examination methodologies. The chapter moves from foundational definitions through a technique-by-technique comparison to ethical and future considerations, and is intended primarily for forensic medicine trainees, pathologists, and medico-legal professionals.

items.title: PGNexus-AI: An Intelligent and Secure Natural-Language PostgreSQL Administration Framework
items.abstract: Modern teams depend on PostgreSQL for mission-critical workloads, yet administration is still done by hand-writing SQL in disconnected tools such as psql, pgAdmin and DBeaver, while AI assistants such as GitHub Copilot have no live connection to the database and cannot read its schema, execution plans or error output. LLM-generated SQL also introduces new injection-style security risks. This paper presents PGNexus-AI, a PostgreSQL-only desktop IDE that combines Google Gemini, Gemma 4 and GitHub Copilot behind a schema-grounded orchestration layer. It provides natural-language-to-SQL generation, execution-plan-driven query optimization, automatic error diagnosis and correction, and AI-generated schema documentation with column-relationship mapping. A defense-in-depth safety layer (parameterization, query preview and confirmation, read-only and sandbox execution, role-based scoping and injection screening) protects production databases, and GitHub integration version-controls SQL and migrations. We describe the architecture, methodology and an evaluation plan covering efficiency, reliability, optimization and security.

items.title: Pharmaceutical Quality Assurance: Principles, Regulatory Framework, Current Practices and Emerging Trends – A Review
items.abstract: Pharmaceutical quality assurance (QA) is a comprehensive and systematic approach designed to ensure that medicinal products consistently meet predetermined standards of quality, safety, identity, strength, purity and efficacy throughout their intended lifecycle. The contemporary pharmaceutical industry has moved beyond a predominantly end-product testing model toward integrated, science-based and risk-based quality management. Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), Pharmaceutical Quality Systems (PQS), Quality Risk Management (QRM), Quality by Design (QbD), validation, qualification, change control, deviation management, corrective and preventive action (CAPA), supplier qualification, documentation and data integrity constitute major components of modern pharmaceutical QA. International regulatory frameworks developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and other regulatory bodies increasingly emphasize lifecycle management, continual improvement and reliable data. The 2024 tenth edition of the WHO pharmaceutical quality assurance compendium provides an updated global framework extending from pharmaceutical development and manufacturing to quality control and post-marketing surveillance. Recent advances in digitalization, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), Process Analytical Technology (PAT), continuous manufacturing and advanced data analytics are further transforming pharmaceutical quality management. However, these technologies also introduce challenges related to validation, data integrity, cyber security, model governance and regulatory acceptance. This review discusses the fundamental concepts, major components, regulatory framework, implementation strategies, current challenges and emerging trends in pharmaceutical quality assurance. An integrated lifecycle-based QA system supported by scientific understanding, risk management, robust documentation, quality culture and appropriate technology is essential for ensuring consistent product quality and protecting patient safety.

items.title: Pharmacogenomics and Personalized Medicine: Translating Genetic Variation into Precision Therapeutics
items.abstract: Interindividual variability in drug response represents a persistent challenge in clinical pharmacology, contributing to therapeutic failure and adverse drug reactions (ADRs) in a substantial proportion of patients. Pharmacogenomics, the study of how genomic variation influences drug disposition and effects, has emerged as a transformative discipline bridging pharmacology and genomics.This review synthesizes contemporary evidence regarding the principles, clinical applications, technologies, and implementation frameworks of pharmacogenomics within the broader context of personalized medicine. Genetic polymorphisms affecting pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic pathways—particularly within cytochrome P450 enzymes, thiopurine methyltransferase, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, and human leukocyte antigen loci—demonstrate robust associations with drug efficacy and toxicity. Regulatory agencies including the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) have incorporated pharmacogenomic biomarkers into drug labeling, while the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) and the Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group (DPWG) have issued actionable dosing guidelines for numerous gene-drug pairs. Despite compelling evidence, the transition from research to routine clinical practice remains heterogeneous globally, impeded by economic barriers, educational gaps, and ethical complexities surrounding genetic data.The integration of artificial intelligence, multi-omics platforms, and digital health infrastructure promises to accelerate pharmacogenomic adoption, yet successful implementation requires harmonized regulatory standards, equitable access across diverse populations, and systematic healthcare professional education. Pharmacogenomics stands poised to fundamentally redefine therapeutic paradigms, shifting from empirical prescribing to genotype-directed precision medicine.

items.title: Philanthropic landowners and what drives them: lessons from implementing nature-based solutions on private land
items.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NBS) are a promising strategy for building climate resilience, but their implementation requires land. Realising NBS on private land, which holds great potential, remains a challenge. Aligning landowner interests with climate adaptation goals lies within the realm of land policy. However, studies show that traditional land policy instruments are often ineffective when applied to NBS and private land. Cooperative approaches that engage landowners directly are needed – but they raise new questions: How do we find landowners willing to implement NBS and engage them effectively? This research focuses on landowners who are primarily motivated by non-financial interests to implement NBS. These dynamics are explored through a qualitative case-study-based research design, focused on NBS implementers across Austria, Czechia, Germany, Italy, Romania, and Slovakia. Initial results indicate different types of landowners (homeowners, farmers, company owners) have distinct interests in implementing NBS. While economic incentives play a role, intrinsic motivations mainly shape landowners’ decisions. This underscores the need for tailored solutions considering diverse intrinsic motivations. Effective NBS implementation strategies must strengthen intrinsic motivations, build trust, and respect landowner autonomy.

items.title: Physical Nudging: Effects of Adherence to Physical Activity Guidelines on Physical Fitness and Self-Management Capacity in Young Adults with Type 2 Diabetes
items.abstract: This study examined the effects of physical activity (PA) guideline adherence on physical fitness, hypoglycemia awareness, and glycemic control in young adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), framing PA adherence as a behavioral nudge toward selfmanagement. METHODS:This cross-sectional study analyzed 108 young adults with T2DM (aged 20-44 years), categorized into two groups based on PA guideline adherence: those meeting guidelines (G-Met; ≥150 min/week of moderate-to-vigorous PA, n=52) and those not meeting guidelines (G-Unmet; <150 min/week, n=56).Lower-body muscle strength, flexibility, hypoglycemia awareness, and HbA1c levels were assessed.Between-group differences were examined using independent t-tests, and independent predictors of HbA1c and hypoglycemia awareness were identified via multiple linear regression. RESULTS:The G-Met group demonstrated significantly greater lower-body muscle strength (p=.003) and flexibility (p=.018) compared with the G-Unmet group.Additionally, the G-Met group reported significantly higher awareness of hypoglycemia causes, including excessive PA (p=.037) and insufficient food intake (p=.014).Multiple linear regression confirmed that PA guideline adherence was independently associated with higher hypoglycemia awareness (p=.021).Although HbA1c levels did not differ significantly between groups, multiple regression analysis identified lower-body muscle strength as a factor independently associated with lower HbA1c (β=-0.343,p=.043).CONCLUSIONS: Adherence to PA guidelines was associated with improved physical fitness and greater hypoglycemia awareness in young adults with T2DM.Importantly, higher levels of lower-body muscle strength, associated with PA guideline adherence, were independently associated with better glycemic control, suggesting that regular PA functions as a behavioral nudge that simultaneously builds physiological capacity and promotes cognitive engagement in diabetes self-management.

items.title: Plausible but Unfaithful? Auditing LLM-Generated Explanations in Cultural Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly recommend cultural venues and tell visitors why, but such explanations can be plausible without being faithful. We report a preregistered counterfactual audit of four commercial LLMs recommending venues in three Greek destinations. Each model received structured visitor profiles based on the ACUX typology and a fixed, fact-checked catalogue of 20 venues, and returned three ranked recommendations with explanations. One profile attribute was changed at a time, and every change was measured against the variation between identical requests (4,032 calls). For every model, attributes cited in explanations were associated with larger changes in recommendations, but only moderately (counterfactual faithfulness score 0.26–0.42). Age, gender and nationality were almost never cited and had small effects that did not survive correction for multiple tests. Explanations often described venue properties absent from the catalogue (29–83%), whereas fabricated visitor preferences were rare (4–14%). When a poorly matching venue was imposed, two models seldom disclosed the mismatch (3% and 13%) and the other two did so in 53% and 79% of cases. Judge-rated plausibility declined only modestly, although agreement with human ratings was low. LLM explanations of cultural recommendations should be treated as persuasive text and checked against the information the system holds.

items.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

items.title: Predict the Reward, Not the World: World Reward Models for ML Agents
items.abstract: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53--62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4--7.5 times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.

items.title: Prediction of postoperative persistent pain after rotator cuff repair based on psychological measurements via machine learning
items.abstract: Abstract Background With the development of artificial intelligence technique, machine learning (ML) algorithms have been widely applied to forecast outcomes of various diseases. Current study aimed to investigate the potential utility of machine learning algorithms for predicting postoperative persistent shoulder pain (PSP) and to investigate the related risk factors following rotator cuff repair surgery. Materials and methods A cohort of 491 patients with rotator cuff tears who had undergone surgical intervention was enrolled and analyzed. Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score of ≥4 at one year follow-up was defined as indicative of ongoing shoulder pain. Consequently, patients were classified into a residual pain group and a pain-free group. Nine commonly used machine learning models were trained to distinguish between patients with residual pain and those without. Furthermore, the three models that exhibited the highest predictive performance were combined into a single ensemble of the nine models to improve the classification of patients with residual pain versus those without. The area under the curve (AUC), specificity, sensitivity and accuracy were calculated for each model to evaluate their predictive capabilities. A prespecified LASSO-based feature-selection strategy was used to identify candidate clinical variables, with additional stability analyses (forward selection, exhaustive search) reported in the Supplementary Materials. Variables consistently selected were considered candidate risk factors for PSP in patients. Results (1) Machine learning models demonstrated their effectiveness in classifying patients with postoperative pain. The predictive performance was notably enhanced using an ensemble learning technique. Among the models, the Support Vector Machine (SVM) exhibited the highest accuracy when serving as the aggregator. (2) The ensemble learning models identified several critical predictive factors, including the Fear of Pain Questionnaire, the Pain Catastrophizing Scale, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)-Perceived Sleep Quality, the Central Sensitization Inventory, and the Pain Surface Body Chart score. Conclusion Our findings suggest that a stacking ensemble of preoperative psychosocial variables, developed and internally validated in this single-center retrospective cohort, shows promise for preliminary risk stratification of clinically significant shoulder pain at one year after rotator cuff repair. These hypothesis-generating results require multicenter external validation before clinical use. Level of evidence Level 4, Diagnosis. Clinical trial number Not applicable. This was a retrospective observational study and was not registered as a clinical trial.

items.title: Preparing for emerging risks: AI, cyber governance, and nuclear security cooperation in Southeast Asia
items.abstract: This Perspective article examines the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) initiatives to strengthen artificial intelligence (AI) and cyber security governance and explores their potential to reinforce nuclear security in Southeast Asia. It argues that as digital technologies become increasingly embedded in nuclear facilities and supply chains, integrating cyber security into nuclear security frameworks is imperative. The study recommends the development of a regional action plan or roadmap to (i) embed cyber security more systematically into nuclear security policies, (ii) deepen cooperation among ASEAN member states, and (iii) raise awareness of the AI–cyber–nuclear security nexus among industry, civil society, and academia. The paper also highlights the roles of key regional and international actors, including the ASEAN Network of Regulatory Bodies on Atomic Energy (ASEANTOM), ASEAN cyber security institutions, AI safety think tanks, and Track II expert networks, in advancing cooperation and knowledge-sharing in this emerging domain. Drawing on the author’s experience with the Nuclear Energy Experts Group of the Council for Security Cooperation in the Asia-Pacific (CSCAP), the paper illustrates how Track II dialogues have facilitated the identification of AI–cyber–nuclear security risks, raised awareness among policymakers, scientists, and academics, and informed ongoing discussions on enhancing nuclear security governance in Southeast Asia.

items.title: PROSE: Rubric-Aware Multi-Objective Fine-Tuning of Small Language Models for Automated Assessment of Second-Language Writing
items.abstract: Automated assessment of second-language (L2) writing supports language teaching and testing by providing rapid, consistent scores across multiple rubric dimensions. We study whether small, openly available language models can be turned into reliable analytic raters, and we introduce PROSE, a rubric-aware, multi-objective fine-tuning method built on a compact DeBERTa-v3 encoder with low-rank adaptation. PROSE trains a regression read-out together with a soft-ordinal auxiliary head, and combines a squared-error term for calibration, a distance-aware soft-ordinal term that respects the ordered rubric bands, a concordance term that restores the spread of human ratings and improves agreement with human ratings, and a trait-relational coherence term. On the ELLIPSE corpus of L2 English essays, PROSE raises the quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.646 for a strong regression baseline to 0.661—a small but statistically reliable gain under a paired test across folds (mean difference +0.015—95% CI [0.007,0.023], and paired t-test p=0.007; p=0.030 after correcting for the overlap between cross-validation training sets), with comparable error and improvements on all seven scoring dimensions, four of which remain significant after Holm correction, and on the Write & Improve (BEA-2019) proficiency data, it matches the strongest baseline on agreement and accuracy and clearly outperforms classification and pure ordinal training. Zero-shot prompting of three strong large language models (GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet-4-6, DeepSeek-Chat) reaches a kappa of only 0.13 to 0.21 on the same essays, and a distributional analysis shows that the tested large models produce compressed score distributions with means below the human mean, while the compact fine-tuned model reproduces the human score distribution. Further analyses show that the gain is stable under reasonable changes of the loss weights and holds for truncated and non-truncated essays and across gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic, and grade groups, although these analyses also reveal a shared grade-related bias and a reliance on length and lexical-diversity cues that call for caution in deployment. The results indicate that, for this task, a task-specific objective applied to a small supervised model is far more effective than general-purpose models used zero-shot; we are careful to attribute the gap to task-specific supervision and objective design rather than to model scale alone.

items.title: Provider perspectives on usability, trust, and adoption of digital health tools under India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission: A qualitative analysis
items.abstract: Background India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is building a national digital health ecosystem. Uptake by health care providers remains uneven. Paper records often persist alongside digital tools, suggesting a gap between tool design and frontline care. Objectives To explore how health care providers and other stakeholders in two Indian states experience the usability of digital health tools under ABDM, how far they trust these tools, and what shapes their adoption in routine practice. Methods We analysed 42 in-depth interviews with state and district officials, frontline health workers, clinicians and implementation partners in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Interviews were collected under the provider adoption objective of the parent Digital Health Exemplars: India study. We used template analysis, with Cognitive Load Theory and Human Factors Engineering as a priori lenses. The themes were then mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Results We identified six mismatches between tool design and clinical reality. These were (1) rigid interfaces that clash with nonlinear clinical reasoning, (2) separate portals that force repeated data entry, (3) fears of surveillance and unclear data use by AI tools, (4) reliance on paper and WhatsApp as practical workarounds, (5) unreliable networks, devices and power, and (6) one-time, generic training. In some settings, use appeared to depend on incentives and partner support. Conclusion Providers in this study did not avoid digital tools because of low digital literacy alone. They avoided tools that added work without clinical value. Sustained adoption under ABDM is likely to need interoperable, offline-capable tools, clear data-use safeguards and cadre-specific training, addressed in national implementation guidance alongside enrolment targets.

items.title: Psychobiotics and polyphenols modulate the gut-brain axis through personalized nutritional strategies in mental health
items.abstract: Anxiety and depression are major contributors to the global disease burden; however, fewer than half of patients treated with standard pharmacotherapy achieve sustained remission. This gap underscores the need to identify effective adjunctive treatments. The bidirectional gut-brain axis offers a valuable perspective by linking diet to neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis reactivity. This framework positions nutritional psychiatry as a complement, rather than a substitute, for established care. This narrative review examines three converging intervention classes: psychobiotics, dietary polyphenols, and precision nutraceuticals. Randomized trials of Lactobacillus helveticus R0052, Bifidobacterium longum R0175, and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128 demonstrate modest but reproducible reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms, although effect sizes vary. Plausible mechanisms include reduced low-grade neuroinflammation, partial normalization of HPA axis reactivity, and a shift in tryptophan metabolism from the kynurenine pathway toward serotonin synthesis—although human evidence supporting these pathways remains limited. Polyphenol biology introduces an additional dimension. Microbial conversion of ellagitannins, isoflavones, and lignans into urolithin A, equol, and enterolactone can alter the bioavailability of neuroactive metabolites. Consequently, an individual’s metabotype likely accounts for some of the variability in clinical response. We propose that microbiota-guided strategies—stratified by enterotype, metabotype, tryptophan–kynurenine flux, and short-chain fatty acid output—could significantly enhance psychiatric care. Multi-omic profiling and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven digital phenotyping can operationalize this precision approach. However, methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, inconsistent strain and dose reporting, and regulatory ambiguity continue to hinder translation, as recent meta-analyses highlight.

items.title: Psychological pathways to responsible generative AI decision-making among teachers: governance clarity, perceived accountability, decision uncertainty, and AI literacy
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can assist teachers with organizing information, generating alternatives, and drafting feedback. Its use in consequential judgments requires verifiable evidence and professional oversight. This study examines how teachers regulate optional GenAI assistance while preserving professional judgment. Methods Research on felt accountability, metacognitive monitoring, and AI literacy is conceptually integrated to develop a psychological process model of teacher decision episodes. Governance clarity is specified through rule clarity and role clarity, with responsible GenAI decision-making defined as regulated decision conduct. Results The conceptual analysis produces five testable propositions and one configurational expectation. Governance clarity is proposed to support responsible conduct through perceived accountability. Decision uncertainty is modeled as a metacognitive signal whose behavioral value depends on calibration and regulation; AI literacy is specified as a resource for verification, calibrated reliance, and appropriate escalation. Responsible conduct encompasses appropriate delegation, verification, calibrated reliance and accountable human authority, traceability, and escalation or override. These model outputs are theoretical propositions, not empirically established effects. Discussion The framework distinguishes generative assistance from conventional algorithmic advice and identifies task-dependent applications in assessment, feedback, referral, and student support. Future tests should compare unaided and assisted judgment, distinguish process quality from decision accuracy, and examine stakes, reversibility, and contextual dependence. Teachers retain authority to accept, modify, or reject GenAI output, or proceed without GenAI assistance.

items.title: Psychometric Calibration of Large Language Models for Multidimensional L2 Academic Writing Assessment: The LICA Framework
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) into Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) has raised pivotal questions regarding their psychometric validity, construct representation, and rater consistency in second language (L2) writing assessment. While LLMs offer scalable scoring and feedback capabilities, empirical evidence regarding their susceptibility to systematic scoring drifts across nuanced analytical criteria remains scarce. This calibration study benchmarks three frontier LLMs—GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro—against an expert human gold standard using the multidimensional LICA framework (Language, Ideas, Cohesion, and Academic Appropriateness). Utilizing a rigorous psychometric pipeline spanning ordinal alignment (Quadratic Weighted Kappa [QWK] and Mean Absolute Error [MAE]), inter-rater reliability (two-way random-effects "ICC" [2,1]), systematic scoring bias (Bland–Altman agreement limits), and multi-rater consensus (Fleiss’ κ), we evaluated model behaviors across a calibrated corpus of L2 academic essays (N total =20 rating instances per model). Empirical findings demonstrate marked dimension-dependent divergence in automated assessment: GPT-4o achieved deterministic concordance with expert ratings ("QWK"=1.000, "MAE"=0.000, "ICC"=1.000, and zero directional bias: d ̅=0.000), faithfully replicating human evaluative criteria. Claude 3.5 Sonnet displayed robust ordinal reliability ("QWK"=0.949, "ICC"=0.966), yet exhibited a systematic leniency drift localized to Cohesion and Academic Appropriateness (d ̅=+0.100, "MAE"=0.100). Gemini 1.5 Pro manifested a pronounced severity drift across Language, Ideas, and Appropriateness (d ̅=-0.250, "MAE"=0.250, "QWK"=0.925, "ICC"=0.947). Crucially, autonomous multi-model consensus reached substantial agreement on overt structural and conceptual dimensions (Ideas: κ=0.643; Cohesion: κ=0.643; Language: κ=0.545), but degraded considerably on Academic Appropriateness (κ=0.286, fair agreement). These results reveal a fundamental construct dissociation: while current generative LLMs reliably evaluate codified linguistic and rhetorical patterns, they struggle to consistently appraise sociopragmatic nuance, epistemic stance, and contextual register conventions. The study cautions TESOL practitioners and assessment developers against treating LLM ratings as monolithic constructs, highlighting the critical imperative of dimension-specific rater calibration and human-in-the-loop oversight in high-stakes L2 writing evaluation and formative automated feedback systems.

items.title: Pure musicking
items.abstract: People learn to play musical instruments in various ways – from being totally self-taught through acquiring skills within the social architecture of friendship groups all the way to training in formal conservatoires. My own journey began with naïve attempts to copy my favourite bands and replicate their music through imitation. Lucy Green’s seminal work How Popular Musicians Learn: A Way Ahead for Music Education (2017) highlights the stark differences between popular and classical musicians in terms of pedagogical approaches, learning environments and music-making processes. Green argues that popular musicians primarily learn through informal, self-directed processes, which contrast starkly with the formalised, structured education which is typical of classical musicians. She notes that popular musicians often start out by playing along with recordings and figuring out songs by ear rather than relying on written notation. This aural tradition emphasises imitation, experimentation and personal discovery, allowing musicians to develop their musicality in a highly personal and intuitive manner. Claire described this organic evolution when recalling the start of her own musical journey: My dad had really good taste in music… . It was through him. I had a record player in my room and I sang. I loved the singing – I sang at school and assemblies. I just remember that from a really young age. I didn’t come from a musical family – none of my family could play instruments – but it was always there. I just knew that I enjoyed it. It was just something that I kept wanting to do. Gloria similarly experienced an irresistible urge to music for its own sake in her youth: I just go back to when I was sitting on my bed when I should have been writing an English essay, noodling on my guitar, writing a song – and it wasn’t to get famous. And it wasn’t for the internet – that wasn’t even a thing. Popular musicians typically engage in what Green describes as ‘enculturation’: a process by which we absorb the music around us, often from a very young age, by listening to and imitating our favourite artists. This process is mostly informal, driven by intrinsic motivation, meaning that we choose what we want to learn and play, rather than anyone else imposing their choices upon us. In other words, we are guided by our own musical tastes and aspirations.

items.title: Quantum-Inspired Pairwise Ranking Aggregation via Active LLM Feedback
items.abstract: Ranking aggregation from multiple retrievers is a powerful yet under-explored technique in modern retrieval and RAG systems. We introduce LLM-IRA, the first extension of the quantum-inspired interactive ranking aggregation framework to document reranking. By leveraging large language models (LLMs) solely for pairwise judgments on high-disagreement document pairs, our method learns fusion weights in a principled, interactive way. The final ranking is a simple, ultra-fast pointwise linear fusion of scores, no full pairwise matrix or expensive listwise prompting is required. Experiments on the BEIR benchmark and TREC Deep Learning tracks with an open-weight instruction-tuned judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) show that LLM-IRA matches or numerically exceeds strong static fusion baselines on 5 of 6 evaluated benchmarks. We report two weight-update variants: momentum blending and a full accumulated-history refit, which together reach statistical significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05) over the best unsupervised aggregator on 4 of 6 benchmarks (DL19 under momentum; DL20, DBpedia, and NFCorpus under accumulated refit, which is the stronger of the two configurations overall). On the benchmarks we profiled (DL19, DL20), it already clears the best unsupervised baseline within as few as 5 LLM calls per query, well before exhausting its typical ~25--30 call budget. LLM-IRA also achieves cost-effectiveness comparable to state-of-the-art zero-shot LLM rerankers at an order of magnitude fewer LLM calls, and requires no training data or model fine-tuning.

items.title: QUIET Care: A Nursing‐Led Conceptual Analysis of Alarm‐Related Acoustic Burden in Adult Critical Care
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult intensive care units (ICUs) generate a persistent acoustic burden from alarms, care activity, equipment and communication. This burden can undermine patient rest and contribute to alarm fatigue, cognitive workload and distress among nurses. AIM: To present a nursing-led conceptual framework for addressing alarm-related acoustic burden in adult critical care. STUDY DESIGN: Literature-informed conceptual analysis. A structured purposive evidence map was audited using two PubMed searches run on 9 September 2026 (3377 unique records after PMID deduplication) and citation checking. Twenty-nine selected sources were charted against the five domains. This was not a systematic review; no original data, formal consensus or framework validation was undertaken. RESULTS: QUIET Care proposes five connected practice domains: quantify and qualify the sound environment; use patient-specific monitoring and alarms; integrate quiet into workflow; engage people and culture; and track, test and learn. It treats the domains as locally adaptable hypotheses and requires explicit safety balancing measures. CONCLUSIONS: QUIET Care is a pragmatic proposal for local co-design and evaluation, not a validated intervention or universal sound target. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: The framework may help critical care nurses and leaders organise source mapping, alarm customisation, workflow redesign, team ownership and small safety-monitored tests of change while preserving the audibility of urgent alerts.

It also propose a five-level system for arranging tasks, calculatingtrust, keeping human control, and checking ethics. The framework is studied using three case studies about customer support,management consulting, software development. It looks at tradeoffs, effects on workers, and rules. The evidence shows that whentasks are easy for AI, can be changed beyond what AI can do, and always need human checks, there are big benefits. items.title: Reference Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) technology has revolutionized the digital marketing sector, yet its impact on consumer psychology requires deeper understanding. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach based on the Scopus database, this study analyzes the relationships among GenAI usage, customer engagement, and customer trust. Literature mapping reveals that current research focuses on four primary clusters: consumer behavioral dynamics and purchase intentions, visual quality (hyperrealism), transparency and ethical issues, and collaborative creativity efficiency. Based on an analysis of these findings, the study identifies an "Authenticity Paradox," wherein AI-generated hyperrealistic visuals effectively boost purchase intentions but risk triggering the "uncanny valley" effect thereby undermining consumer trust if transparency is lacking. Trust is significantly shaped by the interplay between drivers, such as transparent labeling (watermarking), and inhibitors, such as visual artifacts and privacy concerns. Regarding engagement effectiveness, AI proves superior in stimulating interaction among existing followers, whereas human-generated content remains essential for reaching new audiences due to its empathy and emotional resonance. The study concludes that adopting a hybrid marketing strategy specifically Human-AI Co-Creation represents the optimal approach for synergizing GenAI's technological efficiency with the authenticity of the human touch in the long term.

items.title: Reflections on the management of literary works with educational content for the development of the personality of university students
items.abstract: The education of university students requires strategies that link literary reading with personality development. Objective: To present reflections on the management of literary works with educational content for the personality development of university students, based on articles from partner journals—the Cuban Journal of Information Sciences in Health and Islands—located with the support of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and compared with academic literature. Methodology: A qualitative, descriptive-propositive approach was adopted. The proposal was evaluated through consultation with eight professionals in the educational field, including teachers and administrators, intentionally selected for their experience in higher education, reading promotion, and academic management. Results: The reflections were organized into four dimensions: reading and educational diagnosis, selection of works with educational content, planning and allocation of resources, and evaluation of educational outcomes. The proposal highlights the need to coordinate libraries, faculty, and administrative teams to promote reading practices linked to values, empathy, self-esteem, and critical thinking. Conclusion/Contributions: The educational management of literary works can contribute to the development of university students' personalities when accompanied by clear objectives, teacher guidance, administrator participation, and periodic evaluation.

items.title: Reforming General Academic English: a public-health-themed curriculum for Chinese medical students
items.abstract: Public health is an interdisciplinary system that integrates natural science, social practice, and humanistic concepts, committed to safeguarding the population-wide health of society. The global public health crisis triggered by COVID-19 has further pushed public health education into a core position of higher medical education, and integrating public health perspectives into general courses has become a critical trend of disciplinary integration. As a transitional bridge connecting general English and medical English for Specific Purposes (ESP), General Academic English (GAE) at Shandong Medical and Pharmaceutical University (SDMPU) undertakes multiple educational missions: improving students' academic English literacy, fostering autonomous learning competence (1), and meeting national talent cultivation requirements that emphasize humanistic awareness, global vision and international communication capabilities (2).Integrating public health themes into GAE serves as a targeted curriculum optimization approach, which effectively bridges medical humanities and public health expertise, and responds to China's New Liberal Arts initiative launched in 2019 (3). The initiative aims to break traditional disciplinary boundaries and promote interdisciplinary thinking to cultivate high-level compound medical talents.After years of iterative teaching practice, the public-health-themed GAE curriculum at SDMPU has formed preliminary interdisciplinary features. Nevertheless, reflective curriculum analysis indicates that the current teaching arrangement still fails to fully achieve the intended interdisciplinary educational goals. Multiple structural, organizational and practical limitations constrain the curriculum's interdisciplinary cultivation effects. Based on long-term front-line teaching observations and a systematic review of relevant domestic and international studies on medical academic English and public health pedagogy, this paper argues that targeted curriculum reconstruction is necessary to better align GAE instruction with contemporary educational demands, and the institutional talent training positioning. The public-health-themed GAE course examined herein is a 1.5-credit elective offered in the fourth semester for second-year undergraduate Clinical Medicine (Bachelor of Medicine -5-year program) students. Cohorts for this elective typically include approximately 700 students. The course is coordinated by one dedicated overall coordinator and delivered by five English instructors with academic backgrounds in linguistics or literature, each permanently assigned to a fixed teaching chapter; no public-health specialists participate on a regular basis. The course comprises 32 wholeclass in-person lecture hours throughout the semester; small-group activities are embedded within lecture sessions, with no separate dedicated tutorial time, and self-paced pre-class MOOC materials are assigned as out-of-class preparation and are therefore excluded from the 32 contact hours.Assessment consists of one formal final examination weighting 60% and continuous assessment weighting 40%; within the continuous component, group assignments account for 20% and individual assignments for 80%. Core thematic coverage encompasses health governance, nutritional health, genetics, mental health, and traditional Chinese medicine. A concise overview of key programmatic features is provided in Table 1 for cross-institutional reference.This opinion article builds its curriculum reform arguments upon three interrelated theoretical and policy foundations: ESP curriculum design principles, the interdisciplinary philosophy of China's New Liberal Arts initiative, and community-centered perspectives in public health education. In addition, it adopts a normative analytical approach guided by Kern's six-step curriculum development framework.First, ESP principles advocate the integration of language skill training and disciplinary content learning, focusing on context-specific professional communicative needs rather than generalized language instruction (4). Second, the New Liberal Arts initiative promotes cross-disciplinary integration to cultivate compound talents capable of coping with complex social and public health challenges (5). Third, community-centered public health education emphasizes scenario-based practice and real-world problem-solving, encouraging classroom knowledge transfer into authentic community health contexts (6). To clarify, this opinion article analyses an existing course for iterative improvement instead of presenting a de-novo full-cycle curriculum-development project. We therefore treat Kern's framework as an informing reference rather than the strict organisational backbone of the manuscript.We adopt the current structure (curriculum characteristics-dilemmas-reconstruction pathways), which better fits our analytical focus on describing the course status quo and diagnosing implementationrelated challenges. Key elements from Kern's steps are discussed across corresponding sections, while full iterative execution of the six-step cycle is reserved for future practical curriculum delivery.Beyond these overarching foundations, three supplementary analytical lenses are adopted for targeted analysis in subsequent sections. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) provides a framework to examine learner motivation and barriers to engagement. The Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework guides the design of AI-enhanced interactive learning activities. Programmatic Assessment underpins the multi-stakeholder, process-oriented evaluation system proposed for curriculum reconstruction. These three lenses serve as specialised analytical tools embedded within the broader Kern-guided curriculum analysis. The interrelationships among these theoretical foundations and analytical lenses are visualised in Figure 1. The characteristics outlined in this section describe the intended formal curriculum design of the public-health-themed GAE course, representing its structural and thematic aspirations. This section addresses four core attributes: interdisciplinary integration, popular science-oriented curriculum design, diversified blended learning arrangements, and cultivation of cross-cultural critical thinking.Nevertheless, gaps remain between curricular design intentions and day-to-day instructional delivery;these practical implementation challenges are analysed further in Section 4.The public health-oriented GAE curriculum transcends the narrow boundaries of conventional language teaching and integrates interdisciplinary knowledge across public health, clinical nutrition, basic medical sciences, genetics, psychology and medical humanities. Different from general English courses that focus merely on linguistic competence, this interdisciplinary embedding enriches students' systematic knowledge of public health and fosters their multidimensional cross-disciplinary thinking, enabling learners to interpret medical and public health issues from multiple perspectives beyond pure language acquisition.The textbook system of this GAE course at SDMPU takes public health popularization as the main thread throughout curriculum design. It covers a wide range of authentic and practical public health themes, including disciplinary origin debates, cutting-edge medical technologies, and prevalent public health challenges such as dietary-related diseases, nutritional imbalance, and mental health disorders. Key professional public health vocabulary is annotated and interpreted in the textbook, taking into account the dual attributes of language foundation and popular science dissemination.This design aligns with the positioning of GAE as a transitional bridge course between general English and specialized medical English.In terms of teaching organization and implementation, the GAE course adopts an online-offline blended learning model supported by a professional MOOC platform, which realizes full-cycle teaching design covering pre-class preview, in-class thematic expansion, and after-class knowledge consolidation. The course is jointly delivered by a professional teaching team, who adopt differentiated and diversified instructional strategies according to different thematic chapters.Multiple teaching forms, including traditional classroom lectures, flipped classroom tasks, thematic group presentations, and collaborative academic workshops, are flexibly applied in teaching practice.Such diversified blended learning designs seek to enrich classroom teaching scenarios, stimulate students' learning initiative, and enhance learners' proficiency in public health English.In curriculum content arrangement, comparative reading materials are adopted to trigger critical thinking regarding transnational public health governance. For example, thematically paired English texts concerning Chinese and American healthcare systems are introduced in routine teaching. Such comparative reading enables medical students to intuitively analyze institutional differences in public health governance across countries, reflect on the practical dilemmas and optimization directions in global public health development, and integrate linguistic training with humanistic and international public health cognition. This instructional design helps students avoid simplistic, stereotyped perceptions of global public health issues and gradually develop objective, critical and globalized public health literacy. These comparative reading activities aim to foster students' intercultural communicative competence (9) and cultural humility (10), which constitute core dimensions of established global health competency frameworks. Beyond improving basic academic language proficiency, such comparative materials encourage medical students to recognize diversified international public health contexts, embrace cross-cultural differences, and build global-minded perspectives for future professional cross-cultural health communication.While the GAE course possesses promising design-related characteristics laid out in Section 3, gaps between formal curriculum intentions and practical instructional delivery give rise to multiple implementation-level dilemmas that restrict the expected interdisciplinary teaching effectiveness.This section examines these practical challenges across four dimensions: insufficient learning and teaching motivation, fragmented team teaching and overloaded group assignments, disjointed blended learning, and limited social practice opportunities.At SDMPU, General Academic English is set as an elective course, which brings structural challenges for learning motivation. As documented in existing pedagogical studies (11), electivecourse status may shape learners' course-selection priorities. From the authors' front-line teaching observations, some students may prioritize credit completion when selecting electives and may allocate comparatively less time and energy to GAE compared with compulsory medical majors, with superficial engagement in homework and classroom tasks observable among a subset of learners.This practical concern resonates with the core argument from SDT, which highlights how contextual factors and motivational regulation shape learners' perceived autonomy and quality of engagement (12). The elective attribute may also create challenges for consistent teaching standards. Formative evaluation relies heavily on group assignments lacking standardized supervision mechanisms. Based on the authors' teaching observations together with published literature, free-riding behaviors can occasionally emerge within learning teams (13), which may reduce the expected training benefits of collaborative tasks.The rotational team teaching model, in which different instructors are responsible for separate chapters, may bring notable practical trade-offs despite diversifying classroom practice. From the authors' front-line teaching observations, frequent instructor handovers can lead to fractured logical coherence across chapters and inconsistent instructional rhythms, imposing ongoing adaptation pressure on students exposed to divergent teaching styles. Meanwhile, over-reliance on group assignments may add substantial workload for medical students, who are already occupied by intensive professional coursework. As also highlighted in existing relevant literature (13), poorly designed group-based tasks may create conditions raising potential risks of academic misconduct including plagiarism of group assignments.Although flipped classroom and MOOC resources are formally incorporated, the overall teaching logic still leans toward traditional offline lecture-centered models, which may limit the complementary value of online resources. Common practical problems include outdated, lowmatching MOOC materials disconnected from classroom themes, and most instructors take offline teaching as the absolute core while online resources only serve as superficial add-ons without systematic integrated design (14). The separation of online knowledge input and offline practical training can render the blended-learning framework partially nominal in practice.Public health education emphasizes community participation and real-scene problem-solving, enabling students to apply disciplinary vocabulary and logical thinking to solve real social health challenges (15). However, constrained by traditional classroom-centered teaching concepts, the practical activities of the current GAE course at SDMPU are limited to campus-based tasks such as poster design. There is a lack of extended off-campus social practice targeting community residents, foreigners and public health service institutions. The disconnection between classroom theoretical learning and real public health scenarios may create a notable gap between curriculum design goals and practical teaching outcomes. To achieve these learning objectives, curriculum content can be enriched with interdisciplinary resources. Rooted in the multi-dimensional integration logic of public health education covering biomedicine, social science, environmental governance and medical ethics (16), GAE may seek to expand curriculum content with cross-domain resources such as medical resource allocation, occupational health and environmental public health, and embed historical humanistic materials to enrich thematic depth.Two core transformation directions may be identified in curriculum positioning: shifting from single discipline-oriented language training to social demand-oriented interdisciplinary talent cultivation (17), and integrating ideological and political education throughout all thematic modules. Teachers can design diversified off-campus practical activities closely linked to public health themes:producing English popular science videos, delivering community public health lectures, participating in Model United Nations debates on global health, and surveying the application of English public health signs in local medical institutions. These practices may help strengthen medical students' social responsibility and support the fundamental educational goal of fostering virtue through teaching (18,19).As a fundamental institutional guarantee for constructing a stable interdisciplinary blended learning system, SDMPU may consider upgrading GAE to a compulsory course to mitigate motivational deficits originating from the elective-course positioning. Such institutional adjustment may elevate the course's institutional status, help raise students' awareness of the course, and enhance instructors' teaching dedication. With improved curriculum positioning, both students and teaching staff may maintain more sustained and effective engagement, helping lay a solid institutional foundation for standardized, high-quality interdisciplinary blended teaching and public health English training.To address instructional fragmentation caused by frequent instructor handovers in rotational team teaching, SDMPU may establish a fixed core teaching team to unify instructional logic, textbook standards and assessment requirements, thereby reducing repeated adaptation burdens for students. In response to the interdisciplinary requirements of the New Liberal Arts initiative, medical English instructors and clinical and public health specialists can form long-term collaborative teaching communities. Professional physicians deliver instruction on core public health thematic knowledge, while language instructors focus on academic expression, poster composition and international communication skills. Drawing on mature interdisciplinary teaching practices from Capital Medical University (20), this dual-instructor collaborative model may support both professional accuracy and satisfactory language training outcomes (21).To restructure the nominal blended-learning model, the proposed curriculum adopts a project-driven blended-learning design grounded in the CoI framework, which conceptualizes effective onlineoffline education through three interrelated presences: teaching presence, social presence, and cognitive presence (22). Within the GAE curriculum, pre-class MOOC learning supports individual knowledge acquisition; in-class project-oriented, public-health-themed tasks foster peer interaction and collaborative inquiry, while targeted instructor guidance sustains coherent teaching presence throughout the whole learning cycle.The blended learning system realizes rational functional division and organic coordination between online and offline instructional links: online MOOC platforms support pre-class theoretical learning, case reading, and autonomous knowledge sorting (23), while offline classroom sessions focus on project-based practical tasks centered on authentic public health themes (24). Taking the "Diet andHealth" chapter as an example, instructors can design diversified group projects oriented to public health science communication (25). Specific tasks include producing bilingual health popular science videos (26), designing publicity posters for foreign-resident communities, and participating in themed international debate activities (27). To optimize learning outcomes, instructors may moderately adjust the proportion of group assignments and individual tasks to balance student workload. Such flexible arrangement helps alleviate excessive academic pressure on medical students and mitigate potential risks of superficial learning and academic misconduct. Through systematic online-offline integration and well-structured project design, students are able to apply academic English competencies in authentic public health communication scenarios, gradually cultivating the international communication capacity required for future participation in global health governance.Additionally, widely accessible generative AI translation tools bring new pedagogical considerations to this English teaching context. Although AI translation offers convenient linguistic support for medical students, over-reliance on machine translation may hinder vocabulary retention and the development of independent English expression (28). In this GAE curriculum, instructors may adopt balanced strategies: designing offline output tasks without translation tools, prioritizing active language production in authentic public health communication activities, and embedding guidance on proper AI tool use within teaching. First, weights for online and offline assessments may be rationally allocated (30): online platforms leverage big data to record students' autonomous learning trajectories for formative assessment (31), while offline evaluation centers on classroom engagement, group project progress and practical performance. Second, targeted evaluation criteria may be developed for public health practice activities. Relevant references include mature indicator frameworks for medical popular science video assessment (32) and standardized English public signs in hospitals (33); alternatively, task-specific evaluation dimensions can be developed according to the features of each project task. items.title: Reframing Anthropometry and Ergonomics Beyond the Normative Body
items.abstract: Within interior architecture education, anthropometry and ergonomics constitute foundational domains of knowledge for understanding the relationship between users and designed environments. Their pedagogical application often positions the user as a body to be measured, proportioned, and accommodated within space. This study recasts that initial framing by asking how these domains can be taught beyond the normative body and how they may support a relational understanding of user, action, object, and space. The study was conducted as part of an undergraduate course, Ergonomics in Interior Architecture, at Özyeğin University during the Fall 2024–2025 semester; through an active learning exercise structured around role-playing, a case study, and a poster session. The study was conducted in the Ergonomics in Interior Architecture course at Özyeğin University during the Fall 2024–2025 semester through an active learning exercise structured around role-playing, a case study, and a poster session. Students created fictional users with non-normative bodies, mapped their daily routines, and developed spatial and furniture proposals responsive to their abilities, limitations, and needs. The research material comprised the project posters and written reflections of 10 students who completed all stages of the exercise. The data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. The findings indicate that the students moved beyond the procedural application of anthropometric and ergonomic standards, interpreting bodily difference as a generator of design reasoning. The study suggests that by centering a non-normative user in a design problem, anthropometry and ergonomics can move beyond their conventional role as instruments of fit and become pedagogical means through which students learn to understand interior space as a relational field.

items.title: Regulating the Future of Surgery: A Comparative Global Review of Approval Pathways, Safety Standards, and Compliance for Robotic Surgical Systems: A Comprehensive Global Policy, Regulatory Framework, and Risk Assessment Review
items.abstract: Robotic Surgical Systems (RSS) have fundamentally transformed modern clinical therapeutics by enabling unprecedented precision, minimally invasive dexterity, and enhanced 3D visualization. However, the convergence of complex mechatronics, autonomous software algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and telesurgery presents unprecedented regulatory, ethical, and clinical risk profiles. This comprehensive review provides a rigorous comparative analysis of global approval pathways across four major jurisdictions: the United States (FDA), the European Union (EU MDR), Japan (PMDA), and India (CDSCO). We examine pre-market medical device classification, substantial equivalence standards, clinical evaluation requirements, cyber-security paradigms, post-market surveillance (PMS), and surgeon credentialing compliance. Furthermore, this paper critically addresses emerging regulatory hurdles surrounding generative AI integration, autonomous robotic navigation, liabilities in telesurgical latency, and data privacy frameworks. Recommendations are offered for establishing globally harmonized regulatory standards and adaptive oversight protocols to safe-guard patient safety while fostering technological innovation.

items.abstract: A representative transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement system illustrates a high-risk structural-heart technology that enables replacement of the native tricuspid valve without conventional open-heart surgery. A system of this kind typically integrates a bovine-pericardial valve, a self-expanding nitinol frame and anchoring architecture, and a transfemoral venous delivery platform. Such devices have received Breakthrough Device designation and subsequent Premarket Approval (PMA) in the United States for patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) despite optimal medical therapy when replacement is deemed appropriate by a heart team. This article reconstructs the generalized regulatory journey for this device category and integrates classification, standards, clinical evidence, market positioning, global harmonization, project management, regulatory risk, human factors, quality systems, and real-world evidence. An illustrative Gantt chart provides a realistic development model for a device of this risk class. items.title: Rennala NSGD: Asynchronous Stochastic Optimization Beyond Euclidean Geometry
items.abstract: The empirical success of matrix-aware optimizers, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and Shampoo (arXiv:1802.09568), highlights the potential of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, including large language model (LLM) training. Despite this progress, the theoretical understanding of stochastic optimization in general normed spaces remains limited, particularly in distributed settings. We analyze minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for smooth nonconvex optimization with respect to an arbitrary norm on a finite-dimensional space. Using the framework of $κ$-regular normed spaces (arXiv:0809.0813), we derive high-probability oracle complexity bounds under a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm. The bounds make the dependence on geometry explicit through the regularity constant $κ$ of the dual space. In the Euclidean case, our bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors. For some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models, it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one. Building on this framework, we introduce Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm, and establish wall-clock time complexity guarantees under fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times. In the Euclidean case ($κ=1$), our bound matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.

items.title: Repositioning language centres and self-access centres in the age of Artificial Intelligence: From resource provision to human-centred mediation
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled established assumptions in language education. For University Language Centres (LCs) and Self-Access Language Centres (SALCs), AI systems offering instant feedback, writing support, language models, and conversational practice raise questions about their distinctive institutional roles. This opinion paper argues that LCs and SALCs should not compete with AI as providers of content or feedback. Instead, they should become human-centred mediating institutions that help learners, teachers, and institutions use AI critically, ethically, and pedagogically. After revisiting their established roles in supporting autonomous and self-directed language learning, the paper argues that AI demands a more cautious understanding of autonomy, as apparent independence may conceal overreliance, weak evaluative judgement, and outsourced cognition (Barrett & Pack, 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2024). It proposes five future functions of LCs and SALCs: AI literacy development, pedagogical curation, ethical mediation, reflective learner advising, and the integration of formal and informal learning. Drawing on the planned Language Education Institute at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, the paper illustrates how language policy, technology-enhanced pedagogy, and human-centred education may be aligned. Ultimately, the value of LCs and SALCs lies in cultivating judgement, agency, accountability, and community.

items.title: Research and Practice on the Construction of a Lightweight AI-Enabled Welding Experimental Teaching and Safety Intelligent Management System
items.abstract: Aiming at the four prominent problems existing in current multi-process welding laboratories, including difficult supervision of teaching processes, high pressure on safety risk prevention and control, fragmented integration of teaching and management, and difficult implementation of intelligent transformation, this paper takes an eight-category multi-process, multi-equipment, and multi-scene welding experimental teaching system as the research object. Adopting the methods of literature research, field investigation, pilot verification and closed-loop optimization, this study constructs an integrated intelligent management system with in-depth integration of teaching and safety, covering the whole experimental process of pre-class, in-class and after-class stages supported by lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Lightweight AI capabilities are deeply embedded in four key links: standardization of teaching procedures, standardization of operational behaviors, evaluability of experimental quality, and early warning of safety risks, forming a low-cost, easy-to-implement, replicable and scalable intelligent management paradigm for engineering experiments. Practical results show that the proposed system significantly improves the standardization, proceduralization and objectivity of welding experimental teaching, strengthens the capabilities of pre-event early warning, rapid disposal and closed-loop rectification of safety risks, and effectively reduces human supervision omissions. It provides a referable practical path for the digital transformation of university experimental teaching and the modernization of laboratory governance capacity.

items.title: Research on the Construction and Practice of AI Literacy Course
items.abstract: Amid rapid generative AI growth, cultivating AI literacy among non-computer science (non-CS) undergraduates is a key higher education reform priority. Drawing on national policies and domestic course experience, this study constructs a five-dimensional progressive AI literacy framework: fundamental knowledge, risk identification, safety awareness, ethical analysis, governance participation. Pedagogically, the course uses an online smart platform for multimodal delivery, case-based teaching, and integrated process-team assessment. In a teaching practice of AI Safety, Ethics, and Governance with 66 non-CS undergraduates (44 valid surveys), results show a moderate positive correlation between classroom interaction and team project quality; students highly value innovative assessments like team projects and self-designed questions, and most gain achievement from work selected as teaching cases. This study offers an empirically grounded, data-driven course design and evaluation framework, filling the general education gap for non-CS students.

items.title: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS -- LLM-Based Simulations of Survey Responses: A Systematic Literature Review and Synthesis of Methods
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in survey research, including to predict, simulate, or impute responses. Despite a rapidly growing interest in applications to create synthetic survey data, the empirical evidence remains fragmented, with substantial variation in research objectives, model architectures, ``persona'' construction strategies, and validation practices. This paper presents a systematic review of 55 studies published between 2022 and 2025 that use LLMs to generate, predict, or impute responses in survey and related attitudinal or behavioral data. The results suggest that LLM-based survey simulation is best understood as a conditional, use-case-specific tool rather than a general substitute for traditional imputation methods and human respondents. We outline concrete steps toward a more coherent evaluation framework, including use-case-specific metric selection, relational alignment as a standard validity check, and greater transparency in model and design choices.
